cells.tense: The structure you set is holding, and the meaning inside it is still alive right now.
cells.ask: Teach one thing you keep by habit to someone who'll use it differently. Stay through the version that isn't yours.
cells.core:
You set the structure, and it holds without needing you in the doorway. What you keep going is alive — people use it, change it a little, bring their own reasons to it. You're not guarding a form. You're hosting one.

That's the harder balance, not the easier one. Holding something open costs more than locking it, because you keep adjusting — adding where it's thin, taking away where it's crowding, letting the people inside it move. That adjusting is the work, and it doesn't show. The structure looks settled from outside. From where you stand it's a thing you're still tuning, and today it's tuned, and the next person can use it wrong.
cells.sheetLine: You're keeping something alive, not just keeping it.
cells.verb: carrying a shared meaning forward — keeping what's been passed down alive and handing it on
cells.place: where the structure you set is the thing other people live inside

cells.tense: You'll be defending the form long after the meaning has left the room ahead of you.
cells.ask: Pick one rule you enforce and drop it in front of the people who keep it. Let the reason surface without your hand on it.
cells.core:
You're holding the form tighter than the thing the form was for. Somewhere ahead is a version where it finally gets done right, and you're living toward that version — correcting, clarifying, making sure it comes out the way it's supposed to. The doing-it-right has become the point.

The sharpest tell is that you'd rather be obeyed than understood. When someone drifts from the practice, what arrives first isn't curiosity about why. It's a tightening. That's not the structure serving the meaning anymore. The structure has started eating it. Whatever you built this to carry is still in there, and it can't breathe through a sealed window.
cells.sheetLine: You're enforcing the shape and the meaning has gone quiet.

cells.tense: You left the framework behind, and you are still working out how to build one alone.
cells.ask: Ask someone who does this differently than you how they decide what to keep. Use one thing they say this week.
cells.core:
There's no shared way of doing things around you, so the deciding falls to you alone. You work out your own method, keep it as long as it works, and when it stops there's nothing to lean on — no old version to check against, no one who does it the same way and could say what they do.

It looks like independence from the outside. What it is, mostly, is that the working sits entirely on you. You're good at seeing how things fit together — that part is there. What's missing is the part where more than one person holds the same thing, and you get to rest inside something you didn't have to start from scratch.
cells.sheetLine: You're rebuilding what you could have been given.

cells.tense: You are already the one people copy, and the account of yourself has not caught up to it right now.
cells.ask: Notice one thing someone has taken from watching you this month. Say it out loud, plain, no hedging.
cells.core:
People are taking things from you. A phrase, a way of handling the bad week, how you keep something going when it would be easier to let it slide — they pick it up and it becomes theirs. You keep describing yourself as just sorting out your own corner.

You didn't decide to teach any of it. That's why it doesn't show up in how you talk about yourself. But the transmission is running — it runs through what you do, not through anything you'd call a lesson. Claiming it isn't vanity. It's accuracy, and it changes what you do next, because a person who knows they're being copied handles the small things differently.

attempts.check: The unsupported claim I'd flag in a draft is that the person is already transmitting meaning to others — the record supports spacing and repetition, but not who is on the other end of it. A reader could reasonably say 'no one is learning anything from me; I just keep the same order going at home.' The ask survives being wrong: making one rule explain itself changes the rule-holder's relationship to it whatever the audience turns out to be. The sentence that serves me more than them is any line that makes 'steward of meaning' sound like a title rather than a description of a Tuesday.
